The backpack hits the floor, and "How was your day?" gets a one-word answer: "Fine." Kids don’t always say what’s on their mind, but a little time and attention may help them open up.

In a recent development, world Children’s Day is a good moment for parents, caregivers, and teachers to ask kids how they’re feeling and listen without trying to fix anything. The day honors children’s rights, including the right to be heard.

Here’s a look at what the day is about, plus a few activities that can help kids feel understood, at home or in the classroom.

Recent findings suggest that world Children's Day is a global day of action for children, run by UNICEF. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 20. This year’s theme is “My day. My rights. My future.” It invites children to tell world leaders what kind of future they want.

According to recent reports, the day celebrates children and the rights they’re born with. In many places, children “take over” high-profile roles in media, sports, and government for the day. Landmarks light up blue to show support for children's rights.

Sources indicate that november 20 marks two milestones for children’s rights. On this date in 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, a statement of shared ideals. Thirty years later to the day, it adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, a treaty that nations can commit to follow.

The Convention sets out the rights every child has, including the right to be safe, to play, and to have their opinions taken seriously. Nearly every country has formally agreed to follow it, and it’s the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.

Countries around the world mark World Children’s Day. Many also celebrate a separate Children’s Day, most notably June 1, International Children's Day.

In a recent development, some countries do pick dates of their own. Turkey celebrates on April 23, and India on November 14. The dates differ, but the idea is the same: it’s a day dedicated to the youngest members of a community.

It has been revealed that you don’t need a substantial event to mark World Children’s Day. A meta-analysis on children and teens linked understanding emotions with better social skills and fewer behavior problems. Kids can build that understanding in everyday moments, like the ones below.

It has been revealed that kids may not know they have rights, but those who learn about them may feel more confident speaking up. UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention explains the rights in plain language.

Try: Read one or two rights together, then ask which feels most important to them.

Not every child has the words for how they feel. Invite them to sketch their day from morning to night, then have them walk you through it.

It has been revealed that if they’re up for it, ask which part they loved most and which part felt hard. A drawing gives kids something concrete to point to as they talk, and that can feel easier than answering a broad question such as “How are you feeling?”.

Try: At home, pin the drawing to the fridge so your child can talk about it again if they’d like. In class, create an “Our Day” wall where kids can choose to share their drawings and spot the moments they had in common.

Sources indicate that when a child melts down, get curious about the feeling underneath. Help them put it into words: “It looks like you’re frustrated that it’s not your turn. Is that right?” Then listen carefully to their answer before you reassure them. “You’re fine” can sound dismissive, even when you mean well. When you talk about feelings this way, kids often learn to do it too.

In a recent development, try: Post a chart of faces showing common feelings where kids can see it, and invite them to point to or say how they feel at the start of the day. Welcome any details they want to share.

💙 Once a substantial feeling has a name, here are coping skills for kids to try.

Set aside a few minutes at dinner or morning circle time for everyone to share one high, one low, and one thing they’re thankful for. Take a turn yourself so kids feel more at ease sharing.

Recent findings suggest that just listen as kids share, and try not to talk them out of a hard feeling. Kids tend to manage feelings better when you respond with warmth instead of brushing them off.

Try: Pass around a talking object, such as a small stuffed animal. Whoever holds it has the floor, grown-ups included.

💙 On Calm, listen to Feel Thankful With Thomas, a four-minute meditation for little ones, or the Gratitude session from the Classroom Mindfulness Tools series.

In a recent development, A few minutes of meditation can be a soothing way for kids to slow down and settle. Sessions can focus on anything from breathing and body awareness to gratitude and kindness, so there’s room to follow your child’s interests or needs. Kids can sit, lie down, or stand, and they can stop whenever they’d like.

Try: Belly breathing is a gentle place to start. Have your child lie down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watch it rise and fall as they breathe slowly.

It has been revealed that 💙 Explore Calm’s Mindfulness for Kids sessions for ages 3–4, ages 5–6, ages 7–10, and ages 11–13. For little ones, try the Calm Your Worries With Percy meditation from the Thomas & Friends Learn to Meditate series.

Reading together gives you some time to connect, and stories can spark conversations about feelings. Kids may find it easier to talk about how a character feels than how they do.

Pick a book where a character is going through difficult feelings, then pause and ask, “What do you think she’s feeling?”.

Try: At home, make the story the last part of your child’s bedtime routine to help them wind down. In class, read a few pages at the end of the day.

World Children's Day is UNICEF's celebration on November 20, while International Children's Day is the June 1 observance held in many countries. Both honor children and their rights, so you can mark either one or both.

The best World Children’s Day activities for kids are often simple ones, such as inviting them to draw their day, holding a family or classroom check-in, or reading a story together. You can do these activities wherever makes sense, and even a few minutes counts.

Recent findings suggest that when we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Industry observers note that even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

Recent findings suggest that this 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Sources indicate that once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

Sources indicate that when it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

Industry observers note that we think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • Industry observers note that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

Industry observers note that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

Sources indicate that that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Recent findings suggest that autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings key for this group.

In a recent development, despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

According to recent reports, however, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

According to recent reports, sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

In a recent development, sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

Industry observers note that compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Industry observers note that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

Gavin R. Stewart, Ph.D., is a senior postdoctoral research fellow at King’s College in London. His work underscores the importance of developing effective resources for autistic adults.

Breaking: 60 mindful Upcoming Year's resolution ideas to try in 2027

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve all been there.
  • According to recent reports, then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine.
  • Recent findings suggest that take a deep breath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve all been there. January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some Fresh Year’s resolutions. You might optimistically think, “You know what? I’m going to be healthier this year! I’m only going to drink on the weekends.”.

According to recent reports, then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine. You’re instantly filled with regret for breaking your resolution and vow to never do them again because they don’t work and are clearly designed to make you feel disappointed.

Recent findings suggest that take a deep breath. Resolutions don’t have to be this substantial set up for failure that feel impossible to keep. They can be as big or as small as you want them to be. We’ve put together a list of 60 mindful resolutions that are less about striving for perfection or making huge changes in your life, and more about slowly helping you to grow and build better habits in an achievable way. Sounds nice, right?

So let’s ditch our list of impossible goals and jump into 60 resolutions that could help you thrive in 2027.

At the end of the year, many of us step back and realize that we feel really disconnected from a lot of the people in our life. We get busy and stuck in our own little world. It’s too easy for connections with our family, friends, partners, or coworkers to dwindle from time to time.

If this sounds familiar, here are 15 resolutions that can help you build more fulfilling relationships so that your support networks are there for you when you need it. (And you’re there for them when they need it too.).

It has been revealed that pro tip: you don’t need to do all of 15. Just try choosing a few that feel good to you and then take some small steps towards adding them into your routine.

Industry observers note that make a habit of giving your full attention to the people who matter most to you. Try planning regular (or semi-regular) family dinners, date nights, or hangs with friends. If you like phone calls, those work great too. (Just make sure you’re fully present!).

When someone’s talking to you, focus fully on what they’re saying instead of thinking about your reply or what you’re going to eat for your next meal (we’ve all been there). Active listening indicates respect to your loved one and can help deepen your bond. If you want to get better at active listening, here are eight techniques to help.

In a recent development, too often, we take those around us for granted, so let the people in your life know you appreciate them. Saying something as easy as, “thank you” or writing a cute little note can let your loved one know how much they mean to you and make them feel good. Who doesn’t want to make their loved one feel good?

If you love them, say it. Life’s too short! Telling someone you love them is powerful and can help you grow a stronger bond. If you have people in your life like a macho uncle or disengaged cousin who have a hard time saying I love you, be the first to jump in and show them that it’s okay to express your affection for one another.

If you notice someone struggling in your life, step in and help. It doesn't need to be revolutionary. It could be helping with laundry or simply being there to listen. Just letting them know that you see their efforts and want to help can make a huge difference.

It has been revealed that relationships are work. And in order for them to work, you need to put time into them. So set a reminder to check in with your loved ones, especially the ones you don’t see often. A quick text or call can do the trick and help you stay connected with your favorite people. And if you have folks in your life who are struggling, or who experience loneliness, make an extra effort to reach out and show you care.

Don’t let misunderstandings grow. When you’re upset with someone, bring it up to them calmly and kindly, and with the goal of finding a solution. It can help to lead with “I feel” statements. And if your feelings are hurt over an innocent misunderstanding, start with, “I know you didn’t mean to hurt my feelings but,” so the other person knows they’re not in trouble and you want to come to a place of understanding.

According to recent reports, this might sound obvious, but if your loved one has good news, show genuine excitement for the good things that are happening for them. We all feel good when others celebrate with us. So send those flowers — almost no one’s going to get mad at you for sending flowers. Sometimes celebrating success for others feels hard if you feel stuck in your life, but by genuinely finding happiness for others, you may feel the glow of that happiness yourself.

Use conversions with others as a time to genuinely disconnect from technology and focus on being together. When you’re spending time with someone, keep your phone in your pocket, in your purse, or somewhere that’s not in your hand. Give your loved one your full attention. This will make them feel seen and it helps you to stay more in the moment and form deeper connections.

Everyone loves to feel seen and valued. Sometimes just surprising someone you love with a small gesture can make their day. It doesn’t have to be major, it could just be showing up to a hang with your loved one’s favorite snack, their preferred coffee drink, or even a small bouquet of flowers. Trying to be better about budgeting? Handwritten cards, or homemade crafts also make lovely surprises.

When someone you care about is struggling, before reacting, take a moment to put yourself in their shoes and understand what they might be going through. This can be a lot easier noted than done, but try to treat them the way you would want to be treated —  with kindness instead of judgment.

💙 If Empathy doesn’t come easy for you, check out this meditation from Tamara Levitt’s Relationships with Others series.

We all have preferences for how we like to give and receive love and it’s so special when the people in our lives make an effort to communicate affection in the ways we most appreciate. So take some time to understand a partner, family member, or friends love languages (here’s an overview of all five and how to identify yours). Showing love in the ways they like can make you closer. (And probably earn you brownie points!).

Say yes to an invite or an activity you wouldn’t normally do. Stepping out of your comfort zone can help you feel energized and open you up to upcoming experiences and learnings about yourself. The one time when it’s okay not to say yes is if you’re establishing boundaries with your emotional energy or time. It’s all about balance!

While saying yes is great (see above), saying no is also important. Make an effort to have healthy relationships with solid boundaries. Tell people what you need, like alone time or limits on work talk. And respect their boundaries too. If all of that sounds tough, check out these six tips to setting healthy boundaries in your relationships.

Humans make mistakes and the best thing you can do is to acknowledge them, learn and grow. So try to take responsibility if you make a mistake. You’ll feel free of guilt and you won’t have to double down on something you probably didn’t mean to do in the first place (like a bad joke that hurt someone’s feelings, or a meeting you were super late for.) A heartfelt apology can mend any damage and show your maturity (these seven tips will help you do it).

Doesn’t it feel like we’re always trying to find a better work-life balance, get promoted, improve our work ethic, and feel more fulfilled with the work we’re doing? That constant desire for some sort of growth or change can be overwhelming and leave you not knowing where to start.

So we’ve put together 15 work resolutions that might be more sustainable and rewarding for you — and will hopefully make the whole process feel less overwhelming.

Protecting your personal time is so vital for avoiding burnout, so decide on clear work hours and stick to them. Try setting a goal for logging off by 6pm or not looking at emails in your off time. If your job doesn’t right now give you the freedom to set these boundaries, chat with your superiors and express your goals where work-life balance is concerned.

It has been revealed that organize your workspace to reduce clutter. A working area that you like (or at least doesn’t cause more stress) can really improve your mood and your focus. Once you reduce the clutter and get rid of any items that aren’t sparking joy, you could mindfully add things that feel good like a plant, photo, or a comfy chair.

Sources indicate that large projects can be overwhelming. Try breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps to make them less daunting and help you stay on track. You can also practice time-boxing to keep your focus — here’s how to do it .

Go for a five-minute walk, enjoy a cup or tea, or do a quick stretch. It doesn’t really matter what you do on a break, just that you do something to rest your mind and give your body a little love. Set reminders if it’ll help you remember. (Here are 20 ways to take a mindful break.).

Industry observers note that start each day by identifying your top three priorities. If you focus on the most notable tasks first, this will help you make progress where it matters most. Got a few things on your to-do list that aren’t time sensitive? Resist the temptation to try to get them done when you’re exhausted and bump them to tomorrow when you can focus.

Just like you want to celebrate the achievements of the people in your life, it’s equally crucial to celebrate yourself! Take note of all of your accomplishments. This can help boost your confidence, help you stay motivated, and even make you smile.

Making fresh friends isn’t just for your school years. Make an effort to connect with coworkers or other people in your field. Getting coffee with colleagues can help you build relationships and even help with career growth. You might find that your career is more fulfilling when you have solid relationships with colleagues and coworkers.

In a recent development, work on being clear and concise in emails, meetings, and in conversations. Practicing good communication not only improves your productivity but also helps avoid misunderstandings (these 13 tips can help).

If you’re overwhelmed and juggling too much, look for tasks that can be given to others to make your life easier. This doesn’t mean you’re not good at your job. It just means you're making sure your energy is spent where it’s needed most.

In a recent development, struggling to focus? Single-tasting is where it’s at. Take on one task at a time and not five at once. This will improve the quality of your work and help you feel less like you want to scream.

Even if it’s scary, seek out feedback from your boss, coworkers, or clients. Constructive input can help you get better and show that you want to improve. Just make sure you’re also receiving feedback for things you’re doing well, not just areas where you could do better.

Recent findings suggest that find a method that helps you stay on top of deadlines. A to-do list app, a daily planner, or a bullet journal could help keep track of all your tasks. Explore some different ideas to find what works best for you.

Sources indicate that don’t hesitate to ask for what you need. If anything, this can help you get taken more seriously and help with career growth. Ask for that raise, request that more flexible schedule, tell your boss you need additional resources to complete that project.

💙 Learn how to practice Speaking Up at work with this session from the Mindful Leadership Wisdom Series.

Set goals that align with your long-term dreams and values, not just what you hope to achieve. These could be around building confidence, becoming a more mindful leader, or exploring a new field you’ve always been interested in.

When you don’t feel mentally like you’re firing on all cylinders, it can be tough to even think of what to focus on to help your mental health. We get it — you’re probably already stressed, so making a decision on a resolution to be less stressed might be the last thing you want to (or can) do.

To help you out, we put together a list of 15 small and intentional resolutions that will help nurture your mind and create space for calm and joy in 2027.

(Psst: You don’t have to do all of them. Start with one or two that’ll help you feel more balanced, calm, and connected, and then go from there.).

Industry observers note that write down and reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and experiences each day. This can help you process your emotions and recognize some patterns you have. Journaling is also a great way to practice gratitude.

In a recent development, each day, take a moment to think of three things you’re grateful for. This can rewire your brain to look for the positives in your life. It doesn’t have to be getting a promotion or finding your perfect partner, it can be as small as not burning your bagel today. If you want to find more ways to incorporate gratitude into your days, here are eight ideas to get you started.

Spend a few minutes a day practicing mindfulness. And while this could be a five minute meditation, it could also be a bit of deep breathing on a work break, or just noticing the sights and sounds on your morning walk. Any moment where you become fully present counts!

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help you get better quality sleep (here are six more tips to help you get those Zzzzs). The more rested you are, the more you’ll be able to handle the stress that comes up throughout the day.

In a recent development, nature has a way of calming us down and recharging us, so if it’s possible, try to get outside everyday. It doesn't have to be a massive hike, it can be as simple as walking around your block or even just going into your yard.

Recent findings suggest that this is a big one! Try to gradually reduce the time you spend on your phone, computer, or watching TV, especially before bed. You could read that novel that’s been on your bedside table for ever or catch up with a loved one instead. But take it slow, we know it’s not easy.

Give yourself permission to say no to things that overwhelm or overcommit you. It’s more crucial to protect your energy than to burn yourself out trying to please other people. If saying no is hard for you, here’s 30 ways to do it nicely.

Get in the habit of reaching out to a loved one or a therapist when you’re feeling stressed or overwhelmed. Talking about our feelings can help us feel lighter and even give us a fresh perspective.

A clean environment isn’t just for your desk. Having a clean home can calm you too. So take some small steps to organize your home. You might try doing just one room at a time, it doesn’t need to be all at once.

It has been revealed that schedule regular breaks so you don’t have a meltdown. These pauses can really help you reduce your stress and keep you focused. Grabbing a glass of water, breathing deeply, or gently stretching can all help reset you and give your mind a moment to rest.

Recent findings suggest that treat yourself the way you would your closest friend. Avoid going in on yourself with harsh, critical thoughts and instead say some sweet nothings to yourself. We know this isn’t always easy, so here are eight tips to help you quiet that inner critic.

Start a hobby that lets you express yourself. This can be therapeutic and put you in a better mood. Ever been curious about painting or playing music? Maybe now’s your chance to explore that curiosity.

In a recent development, exercising relieves a lot of stress. But you don’t need to spend hours at the gym or set some significant weight loss goal. Instead, try out a fresh yoga class, have a dance party in your living room, or find other ways to move your body that feel nourishing to you.

Go easy on yourself, you don’t need to be perfect (newsflash: there’s no such thing). It can help to focus on all the small ways you're growing each day, not on the destination. Sometimes it’s better to think about growth-setting instead of goal setting.

Don’t regularly spend your time on something that drains your energy. Seek out places that bring you positivity instead. If certain people you hang around with make you feel bad, limit your exposure to them. This might look like setting boundaries with family about how many events you attend each year, or with friends by limiting how much you talk or get together.

💙 If you’re looking for more positivity in your life, learn how to Process and Move Past Negativity during the Overcome Stress and Anxiety series with Dr. Julie Smith.

Sources indicate that okay, let’s face it. Most of us want to look and feel our best — and there’s nothing wrong with that. But better physical health is also about feeling energized, staying strong, and giving our body the help it needs to thrive.

Sources indicate that we don’t need to tell you that working out consistently is a lot easier mentioned than done. Sure, in a perfect world, we always have the time and energy to get to the gym. But we don’t live in that world. We have endless responsibilities and working out might be the first thing to go when we’re busy.

So explore these 15 manageable resolutions that can help you feel strong and energized going into 2027. And remember, you don’t need to force yourself to go all-in on physical wellness to feel better. Just start with one or two that feel like they’d be easier to make a consistent habit and go from there.

Industry observers note that aim for some form of movement every day –– it doesn’t have to be intense. Try a 10–minute stretch or a brisk walk through your favorite part of your neighborhood. Focus on what makes you feel good in your body, which may change day to day.

Hydration makes you feel good and stay alert, so try to aim for 8–10 glasses of water a day. Carry a reusable water bottle with you to make it easier to hit your goal and remind you to drink. If regular water feels boring try adding slices of your favorite citrus or fresh mint to your water.

Add a rainbow of foods to your plate! Focus on eating a mix of fruits, veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains. Try meal prepping ahead of time to make it easier for you to choose healthy options. Bonus points if you try to stay mindful while you cook and while you eat — here’s how.

Swap out processed snacks for healthier options like fruit, nuts, seeds, or yogurt. Try keeping nutritious snacks nearby to make it easier to avoid reaching your favorite sweets. With that in mind, don’t forget that dark chocolate has some antioxidants so adding a few dark chocolate chips to your trail mix is a-okay with us!

Recent findings suggest that when you sleep better, you feel better. End of story. Aim for around eight hours of quality sleep each night. It can help to have a wind down routine at the end of your day to help your body know that it’s time for rest. These nine steps can help you create a calming bedtime routine.

If you are able to take stairs instead of elevators or escalators, go for it! Making small, active choices throughout your day to help you get a little more movement. You could also try parking farther away to get in a few extra steps.

Add some stretching into your daily routine to improve your flexibility, reduce your tension, and prevent injuring yourself. Try stretching for a few minutes as soon as you get out of bed or right before you get into bed — here are seven we like.

We know it can be frustrating or scary to go see a doctor, but don’t wait to see one until you feel sick. Set up your physicals and dental cleanings so that you can breathe easy and not worry about your health. You’ll be proud of yourself when you leave that doctor’s office!

Sources indicate that generally, it’s recommended to cut back on foods high in sugar. You may be surprised how much sugar some of your daily go-tos have, so stay mindful of what you’re consuming (you could check the labels for sugar content if that works for you).. It’s not about never having a treat, but bringing more awareness to what you’re eating and how it’s making you feel. It’s all about balance.

Industry observers note that working out can really feel like work a lot of the time. So shake up your routine to help keep you excited to exercise. Ever tried kickboxing or swimming? Maybe 2027 is the year you hop in the boxing ring or jump in the pool.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a desk job, try to stand up and move every hour. Consider switching to a standing desk if that’s an option. If you work from home and have space for a walking pad in front of a standing desk you can also get your steps in while you work.

We know that the new year isn’t always the time you want to get outside for a walk, but sunshine and time in nature can boost your mood. If you live in the northern hemisphere, bundle up and try going for a walk, run, or bike ride outside whenever the weather allows it.

If you drink alcohol, consider cutting back by a few drinks or setting limits. It can help to have fun or festive swap, so try sipping on flavored sparkling water or a mocktail at a social event or as a treat at the end of a long week. Sometimes creating a special drink that’s free of booze creates the same excitement as making a special cocktail. And you might love the way you feel the next morning when you’re hydrating your body with your evening beverage instead of dehydrating it.

In a recent development, good posture helps prevent back and neck pain so pay attention to how you sit and stand. And add exercises that focus on strengthening your core into your workout. This will help support better alignment. Sitting at a desk for work? Set alarms every so often to remind you to stand up and stretch.

Industry observers note that celebrating your progress helps you to keep going — we all need a good pat on the back. If you drink an extra glass of water or walk an extra mile, take note of it. Maybe even do a little happy dance. If you go for a walk four days in a row, make a note in your journal or notebook. The more you celebrate your progress the prouder of yourself you’ll be (and the easier it is to keep it up).

💙 Learn how to celebrate the Small Wins on the path to achieving your larger goals with help from Jay Shetty.

New Year’s resolutions are personal goals or promises you make to yourself at the start of a new year. They can be about anything and it’s entirely up to you. They can be substantial like training for a marathon or small like drinking more water.

Recent findings suggest that usually people use it as a chance to reflect, change up some patterns in their life, and start fresh. If you’re looking to set a resolution but don’t know where to start, here are five areas people tend to focus on:.

Sources indicate that you don’t have to make resolutions to have a wonderful new year. But if you want to try, keep in mind that resolutions work best when you make them work for you. So yes — resolutions matter if you use them as a tool to help you live with more purpose and joy, then you’ll set yourself up for more success.

When you’re setting your resolutions, focus on what would make you feel happier, healthier and more fulfilled and go from there. And approach resolutions with kindness and flexibility, especially if you don’t end up following through on one.

Sources indicate that if the idea of resolutions feels overwhelming — we get it. Here’s three ways that could make it easier for you:.

Focus on one word or theme for the year that feels right to you, like “balance” or “growth.”.

Set a small monthly intention instead of a year-long commitment.

Celebrate progress instead of perfection by noticing little wins along the way.

In a recent development, we wish there were five magical resolutions that could solve all of our problems at once. But unfortunately there’s no such thing. What we can tell you is the most successful resolutions tend to be the ones that feel right to you.

It has been revealed that it’s key to focus on the right area when setting your resolution, so you’ll be more likely to stick with them. Here are five areas to focus on when setting your resolution:.

Resolutions that focus on building stronger relationships — Pick ones that’ll fill you up and add more joy to your life.

Resolutions that focus on taking care of your physical health — Pick ones that focus on regular exercise, better nutrition, or improved sleep.

Resolutions that focus on your mental health — Pick ones that practice gratitude or mindfulness, so that they can help you feel calmer and more balanced.

Resolutions that focus on your career –– Pick ones that focus on learning a latest skill or creating a better work-life balance so that your professional life can become more rewarding.

Resolutions that focus on personal growth –– Pick ones that focus on starting newly introduced hobbies or giving back to your community.

According to recent reports, all of us at one point or another have probably failed at a resolution we’ve set for ourselves. And when that happens, it can feel pretty disappointing. But resolutions can work — if you set them in the right way.

Industry observers note that resolutions that are vague or overly ambitious tend to be a recipe for failure. But if you set ones that are realistic and meaningful to you, it’ll be a lot easier to keep your resolution and see the change you want. But remember to be flexible and kind to yourself. We’re all not perfect and mistakes happen. So try not to beat yourself up if you don’t stick to your goals perfectly. Focus on progress, not perfection.

It has been revealed that if you find it easier to set monthly intentions as opposed to setting one year-long resolution, go for that. Tailor the resolutions so they work best for you.

Sometimes the minute we think of resolutions, we can get sad or overwhelmed at the baggage of our past failed resolutions. If this is you — we understand. Resolutions aren’t for everyone. But if you’re interested, there are other ways you can focus on self-improvement and growth.

It has been revealed that if a long list of goals is too daunting for you, try picking a single word to guide your year. You could use words like “balance,” or “connection,” to remind yourself to make choices that match with your values.

If setting smaller, short-term goals might help you to stay motivated, you could try focusing on building better sleep habits in January, and then shifting to something like improving your diet in February.

According to recent reports, if tracking your progress will make it more fun for you and help you to invest more, try using a habit tracker app, or even just a calendar. This way it’ll be easier to celebrate your little wins along the way.

Resolutions that focus on relationships can bring more connection, understanding, and happiness into your life. And a good way to show the people you love the most how much they mean to you is to set a resolution to spend more quality time with them.

Is Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Worth It? The Hidden Costs

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing).
  • BNPL providers make money in two ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Avg Spending Increase with BNPL.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term intends, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

In a recent development, the "interest-free" label on short-term plans deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies indicates that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

The financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

Sources indicate that A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL users have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound quickly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

In a recent development, the credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing aims to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a newly introduced dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

It has been revealed that the financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something crucial.

The question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how quickly you reach FI.

The average ChooseFI listener saves $24,000+ with an expert student loan plan.

Trusted by Brad Barrett, Co-founder and Host, ChooseFI.

Recent findings suggest that mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL plans — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening latest ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing looks report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Recent findings suggest that afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

It has been revealed that klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing plans charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It has been revealed that it is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently demonstrates that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most consumers, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Sources indicate that because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL consumers spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a new job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a new schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

Sources indicate that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Sources indicate that transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A fresh job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

“I don’t travel much,” says Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

It has been revealed that this 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

Sources indicate that and lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

Recent findings suggest that we highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole latest level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

Recent findings suggest that we think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

In a recent development, below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer. We've looked at what each one offers and named what we like about it, so you can decide which one to try.

Before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

The best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:.

What do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

Industry observers note that how much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

In a recent development, how personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

What's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

In a recent development, calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

Content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. You'll also find breathwork exercises, mindful tools, soundscapes, intro courses, and longer programs on themes like anxiety and self-kindness.

Personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

It has been revealed that standout feature: For us, it's the sleep content. Sleep Stories are the first thing we’d recommend to a friend who’s struggling with sleep.

Industry observers note that headspace is another widely-used meditation app, and it leans into teaching. Many sessions are organized into courses that walk you through a topic step by step.

Content library: The app features beginner courses and SOS meditations, short sessions for when stress spikes. It also has themed collections for focus and movement. For sleep, there are Sleepcasts.

Personalization: Headspace offers personalized recommendations and its AI companion, Ebb, lets you talk through how you’re feeling and suggests app content in response.

Standout feature: We like how Headspace gives beginners a clear path to follow, starting with its 10-session Basics course.

Insight Timer started as a meditation timer and grew into a large library of guided meditations, with plenty of free content and a paid tier called MemberPlus.

Content library: The app hosts a catalog of meditations, talks, and music tracks, plus a meditation timer for people who prefer to sit in silence.

Personalization: You can join teacher-led challenges to help you stay on track, and the streak feature tracks how many days in a row you’ve meditated.

Standout feature: We like how much the app offers for free. With so much available, you can try a range of teachers before paying for anything.

According to recent reports, calm won’t be right for everyone, but here’s why we love it. (Keep in mind that this section is our point of view, not a neutral comparison.).

The daily meditations are a great place to start. There are three to choose from, and each has its own feel:.

The Daily Calm, with Tamara Levitt, leans toward gentle reflection.

The Daily Jay, with Jay Shetty, draws on psychology and timeless wisdom.

The Daily Trip, with Jeff Warren, suits curious meditators who like to experiment.

You may click with one voice more than the others, so it’s worth trying all three to find out whether you’re a Tamara, Jay, or Jeff person. (There’s a fourth daily too, the Daily Move, a short mindful movement session — a great way to get your body ready for the day.).

Industry observers note that we’ve also produced a lot of quick meditations over the past few years, all under five minutes. So even the busiest person, or the most skeptical first-timer, has something small to try.

In a recent development, sleep is the other main reason we keep coming back. With our Sleep Stories and nighttime meditations, we’ve unlocked a delightful way to let go of the worries of the day, relax your mind and body, and allow yourself to fall (and stay) asleep easily and naturally. Our 500+ Sleep Stories include some of the world’s most celebrated and soothing voices, like Harry Styles, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Rosé, and Greta Lee. With plenty more to choose from, there’s always something fresh to help you wind down and drift off.

According to recent reports, then there’s how the app looks and feels. The visuals lean into calming nature—think misty forests, rain on a window, slow ocean waves—so opening the app itself sets the scene for calm. And if you just need to tune out the world for a while, our Rain on Leaves soundscape is a legit vibe.

According to recent reports, the numbers back up the impact. More than 180 million people worldwide have downloaded Calm, and its content has been studied in peer-reviewed research. For example, in one randomized trial of 88 stressed college students, those who used Calm for eight weeks reported lower perceived stress than a wait-list group.

In a recent development, they may help, though the research is still young. An updated review of 45 randomized trials found improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms among people using mindfulness apps, compared with control groups. The effects were modest, and the authors note we still need larger, higher-quality studies to say how much apps help and for whom.

Recent findings suggest that an app also isn’t a substitute for professional care. If you’re struggling with your mental health, it’s worth talking to a doctor, who can help you find the right support.

Related read: The science behind Calm: 27 studies and surveys.

Recent findings suggest that yes, though how much is free varies a lot. Calm and Headspace each offer a limited selection of free sessions plus a free trial of their paid looks, with most of the library behind a subscription. Insight Timer works the other way around: the bulk of its catalog is free, with a paid MemberPlus tier for extras like courses and offline listening.

In a recent development, to choose the right meditation app, start with your main goal, whether that’s stress relief, better sleep, or a guided start as a beginner. From there, check prices and any features you care about, like offline listening or language options. Then take advantage of the free trials. Most apps offer one, and it’s a good way to see how an app fits before you pay. While you’re trying it out, sample a few different narrators. A lot of meditation comes down to the voice guiding you, and finding someone you connect with can turn the practice into something you look forward to.

Calm is worth it if you want to ease stress and anxiety, sleep better, focus when your mind wanders, or learn the basics of meditation. The app may be a helpful way to build a daily mental health habit, with support for moments from a racing mind at bedtime to a hard day at work. Whether you need quick relief in the moment or ongoing support through a life change, Calm is for you.

You can try a 7-day free trial to see how it fits your flow, and you don’t need to know which content format you prefer ahead of time.

Calm and Headspace have a lot in common. Both offer guided meditation, beginner-friendly courses, short sessions for when stress spikes, sleep content, and mindful movement. The difference is in the mix and the overall feel. On Calm, you’ll find hundreds of Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, daily meditations from a rotating cast of instructors, music, soundscapes, and Emergency Calm sessions for high-stress moments. On Headspace, you’ll find a more course-led, step-by-step approach and an AI companion called Ebb. Both offer free content and a free trial, so the best way to decide is to try each and see which feels right for you.

In a recent development, mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Substantial Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: New Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

Sources indicate that in clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

In a recent development, “These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

Many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

Recent findings suggest that “This raises a really important question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John noted. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

Recent findings suggest that the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John noted.

Industry observers note that [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

Sources indicate that in doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John said.

John’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she remarked.

For more on ADHD in midlife and beyond, watch the full webinar at additu.de/111726.

If a plain “happy birthday” feels too bare, one extra line does the trick, like naming an inside joke or something you're glad they're around for.

The best birthday message is one that’s honest, reflecting how you feel about the person. Whether it’s a thoughtful one-liner or a whole paragraph, what matters most is that it sounds like you and is from the heart.

In a recent development, to start writing a thoughtful birthday wish, think about what this person brings to your life. Are they the person who makes you laugh when things get heavy? Do they show up when others flake? Start there, and be as specific as possible.

In a recent development, you could even include a shared memory, a personal trait you admire, or something they’ve done recently that made you proud. It doesn’t matter if it’s short or long — just that it’s real and meaningful to you.

If you don't know the person well, start your message by being warm and casual. Something like, “Wishing you a joyful day and a year filled with good things” works perfectly.

If it’s for someone you know in a professional context, try, “Hope your day is filled with appreciation and celebration — you deserve it.”.

You don’t have to fake closeness, but you can absolutely show care.

Sources indicate that this one depends on your relationship with the person. If humor is a shared language between the two of you, you absolutely can. Just pay attention to the tone.

Inside jokes, light teasing, or self-deprecating lines can be great, but if you’re unsure how your humor might be perceived, it’s safer to aim for warmth with a side of personality. Don’t try it if it starts feeling forced.

Let’s be honest. “Happy birthday” gets the job done, but it’s also one of the most basic options. If you want to switch it up, try something a little more personal or playful.

“Celebrating the fact that you exist today!”.

Industry observers note that “Another year of you being excellent. Carry on.”.

“Hope today treats you like the royalty you are (with cake).”.

“Wishing you all the good stuff, and no fine print.”.

You can write a short, warm note that fits how well you know the person. One or two sentences is plenty.

If you’re close, an inside joke can work. If you’re not, thank them for something specific, like their help on a project or the way they greet everyone in the morning. For example, “Happy birthday, Priya. Thank you for always making time to help.”.

It’s usually best to skip jokes about age or appearance, especially in a card other people will read. If a group card is going around, add your name and one line of your own instead of repeating what’s already written.

A short, sincere happy birthday message is one or two sentences that greet the person and share one kind thought. It doesn’t need a joke or a long story to mean something (and it works the same way in a text, a card, or on social media).

Sources indicate that A basic format is the person’s name, “happy birthday,” and one line about them or your hopes for their year. For example, “Happy birthday, Maya. I’m so glad you’re in my life.” Or, “Happy birthday, Dan. Hope this year brings you more rest and more cake.”.

#69199. Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a upcoming study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a upcoming study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

Study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings highlighted that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

According to recent reports, premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

Sources indicate that the study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

Researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

The relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents noted that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

Recent findings suggest that “I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, said. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” stated Connie, another reader.

Recent findings suggest that “I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” mentioned ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

In a recent development, “PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

“Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

In a recent development, the researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors mentioned they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

#69198. How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)
