Breaking: How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game.
  • Recent findings suggest that election season can make the news feel unusually personal.
  • There is even a name for this experience: election stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game. A few minutes later, you have read three election headlines, watched a clip from a debate, skimmed dozens of comments, and somehow learned that democracy, the economy, your health care, and the future of the planet may all be in danger before breakfast.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone.

Recent findings suggest that election season can make the news feel unusually personal. The problems on the ballot can affect our finances, health, schools, communities, and rights. At the same time, the way we now encounter political information—constantly, emotionally, and often in fragments—can leave us feeling overloaded rather than informed.

There is even a name for this experience: election stress. The Mayo Clinic describes it as the overwhelming anxiety some people feel during an election cycle. And surveys from the American Psychological Association suggest that elections have become a significant source of stress for many Americans. In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, for example, 72% of adults said they were worried that the results could lead to violence, and 56% said they feared the election could mark the end of democracy in the United States.

In a recent development, it is understandable to feel unsettled when an election seems to carry serious consequences. But anxiety is not always a problem to get rid of; in small doses, it can direct our attention toward what matters. It may motivate us to learn, vote, volunteer, have difficult conversations, or support people affected by political decisions.

The problem begins when information meant to help us engage instead keeps our nervous systems in a constant state of alarm.

Part of election stress comes from the uncertainty it elicits. We do not know who will win, what policies will change, or how the people around us will respond. Research suggests that uncertainty itself can be stressful because people naturally want to understand and predict the environment around them. When we feel unable to do that, we may feel less safe and less in control.

News can intensify that uncertainty. Negative news is often more attention-grabbing than positive news, and conflict, danger, and outrage make especially compelling headlines. That does not mean journalists are intentionally trying to harm us. Reporting on threats and problems is an essential part of journalism. But a steady diet of alarming information can shape how we feel about the world, especially when it leaves little room for context, solutions, or signs of human cooperation.

This can create a difficult cycle. When people feel anxious, they often seek out more information in an effort to regain a sense of control. Yet the more election news they encounter—particularly news marked by uncertainty, conflict, and emotional intensity—the more anxious they may feel. Then they check again.

In other words, we may turn to the news to calm ourselves down, only to leave feeling more activated than before.

Political stress is not upcoming. But the way we receive political information has changed dramatically.

According to recent reports, when John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon debated on television in 1960, viewers watched in a far more contained media environment. There was no endless stream of clips, reactions, memes, push notifications, and commentary arriving at every hour of the day. People could discuss the debate afterward, but they were not also carrying the debate around in their pockets.

Today, election news can follow us almost everywhere: to the grocery store line, the waiting room, the car, the dinner table, and bed. Social media makes it easier for people to participate politically and amplify voices that were once excluded from public conversation. Those are meaningful benefits. But the same technology can make political information feel impossible to put down.

It also encourages us to consume news in small, emotionally potent pieces. A headline while brushing our teeth. A video clip while waiting for coffee. A dramatic post at a stoplight. These snippets can provoke strong feelings without giving us enough context to understand the story fully.

That matters because headlines often tell us what to feel before they tell us what happened. Pew research found that five out of eight Americans (63%) mentioned they only read news headlines rather than full news articles, specifically when scrolling through social media. When people repeatedly take in emotionally charged fragments of news, they may feel a growing sense of threat while having less detailed information to guide their judgments.

Industry observers note that faced with this constant emotional demand, some people keep checking the news compulsively. Others decide they have had enough and stop paying attention altogether.

It has been revealed that news avoidance can offer temporary relief. If every update makes you tense, angry, or helpless, closing the app may feel like self-protection. In fact, a report from the American Press Institute found that a third of Americans want to disengage from news because it feels stressful and overwhelming.

Tips for managing election stress while building a better democracy.

Industry observers note that but avoiding news altogether comes with costs, especially during an election year. It can make it harder to participate in democratic life, understand issues that affect our communities, or distinguish reliable reporting from misinformation passed along by friends, influencers, or highly partisan accounts.

In a recent development, the goal, then, is not to consume more news or no news. It is to develop a healthier relationship with news: one that helps us stay informed without asking our nervous systems to be on call all day.

1. Choose a news source that includes solutions, not only problems. During stressful times, it can help to seek out reporting that does more than identify what is going wrong. Constructive journalism still covers serious problems, but it also provides context, examines solutions, and asks what people and communities can do next. This approach is not about pretending everything is fine. It is about giving readers a more complete picture: What is the problem? Who is affected? What is being tried? What can citizens realistically do? Solution-oriented reporting may be especially helpful during elections because it can replace helplessness with a more grounded sense of agency and hope for the future.

Sources indicate that when you choose a news source, consider asking: Does this reporting leave me better informed? Does it help me understand the concern, or does it only make me feel alarmed? Does it explain possible solutions as well as the threat?

Industry observers note that 2. Balance distressing news with inspiring media. We do not need to force ourselves to be positive about difficult realities. But we can balance the emotional weight of election coverage with media that remind us of human goodness, beauty, courage, and connection.

Research suggests that stories of kindness, moral courage, and collective care can evoke feelings such as elevation, gratitude, and hope. These emotions can broaden our view of what is possible and help us feel more connected to other people. And new research from the University of Santa Barbara suggests that these emotions can even reduce stress.

This might mean watching a short video about neighbors helping one another after a disaster, reading a profile of local organizers working across differences, listening to music that helps you settle, or returning to a film or show that leaves you feeling more hopeful about people, or nostalgic about the past.

In a recent development, think of this as building a more balanced media diet. Election news can be an crucial part of that diet, but it should not be the only thing we feed our minds. Just as eating one healthy meal a week does not transform our physical health, one inspiring story will not undo chronic stress. Over time, though, regularly choosing media that restore us, physically and mentally, can help cultivate resilience, hope, and perspective.

According to recent reports, 3. Create boundaries around when you check the news. Finally, consider treating news less like a snack and more like a meal.

Snacking on news all day can mean consuming a lot without ever feeling nourished. You absorb a headline here, an alert there, and a few comments in between—but never get enough context to make sense of what you are seeing. The result can be a lot of emotional calories and very little understanding.

According to recent reports, instead, choose one or two intentional times to engage with the news. You might read a full article over breakfast, listen to a trusted news program on your commute, or set aside 15 minutes at lunch to review the day’s major stories. If you are prone to checking headlines compulsively, digital wellness strategies such as app limits or notification settings can make those boundaries easier to keep.

It may also help to avoid making late-night news “snacking” part of your bedtime routine. By the end of the day, our emotional and cognitive resources are often already depleted. A stream of alarming headlines can quickly turn into doomscrolling: the repeated consumption of negative online content that leaves us more agitated and less able to sleep.

Giving news its own place in the day does not mean becoming indifferent. It means making room to take in information carefully, in context, and with enough emotional space to respond thoughtfully.

Election stress is real because elections matter. Feeling concerned about the future does not mean that something is wrong with you; it may mean you are paying attention.

Sources indicate that but paying attention does not require constant exposure to distress. We can choose reporting that informs and empowers us, balance difficult coverage with media that reminds us of human possibility, and set boundaries that give our minds a chance to rest.

According to recent reports, the aim is not emotional numbness. It is becoming the kind of informed citizen who can face difficult news, stay connected to what matters, and still have enough calm and hope left to act.

Recent findings suggest that sophie H. Janicke, Ph.D., is a positive media psychologist working as an associate professor at Chapman University, who investigates the role that new and traditional media play in promoting and affecting character development, self-transcendent emotions (such as elevation, gratitude, and awe), prosocial behavior, and happiness.

#69053. What’s Crucial to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1509 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

What’s Crucial to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy challenges.
  • Sources indicate that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans.
  • Sources indicate that “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” remarked Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy challenges. But a fresh study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

Sources indicate that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of challenges before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

Sources indicate that “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” remarked Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”.

For example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean that people are irrational, said coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”.

Sources indicate that still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar said, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other complications, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

Recent findings suggest that the paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

The foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, plans, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

According to recent reports, while many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

Social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a newly introduced kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

In all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

In a recent development, consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

The computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most notable factor for that participant.

The same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

It has been revealed that the research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

It has been revealed that but that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

Nearly 54% showed a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

Industry observers note that how many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Banavar mentioned, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

Industry observers note that “You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she stated. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”.

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she said.

Recent findings suggest that the study comes with some vital caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

It has been revealed that further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar noted, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

It has been revealed that the authors say their research has vital implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

Sources indicate that often, Bansak said, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The new research shows analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that and that understanding, Banavar noted, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present issues in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really notable to them, given a particular issue? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:.

Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

In a recent development, comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Recent findings suggest that humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

Industry observers note that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

It has been revealed that work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

Industry observers note that subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

Industry observers note that frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an important open question.

According to recent reports, to study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

This finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

In a recent development, can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

Sources indicate that this result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

Such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an key and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Industry observers note that our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

An area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

We now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

According to recent reports, can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

It has been revealed that future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

Finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are currently conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

Recent findings suggest that while we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate blueprint must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:.

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

In a recent development, the FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

It has been revealed that A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

In a recent development, key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

It has been revealed that estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • Middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

Middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

Many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

Research is one notable way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate problems, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

Recent findings suggest that in schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

Recent findings suggest that systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

Relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this concern further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

According to recent reports, student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect latest students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

Our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

Second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the complications that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action plans and recommendations.

Finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or glitch. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these issues, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

Industry observers note that YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

Recent findings suggest that further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an issue or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action looks and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

Throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions prepares and recommendations to address their selected problem.

Sources indicate that A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

Industry observers note that you can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson prepares and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. The YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

Sources indicate that power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

Recent findings suggest that the results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action aims.

One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether upcoming routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

In our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

There is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and Newly introduced Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

Students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

Brian Villa, DrPH, MPH, MSW, is a postdoctoral scholar with the Institute of Human Development at UC Berkeley. He serves as a core member of the San Francisco Unified School District and UC Berkeley Research-Practice Partnership.

Wendell Berry on Where Our Gone Loved Ones Go

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, to love is to sign a contract with loss.
  • When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment.
  • It has been revealed that death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, to love is to sign a contract with loss. To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life.

When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment. “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend.

It has been revealed that death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering where love goes when it goes. At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death.

It has been revealed that all deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life.

That is what the achingly missed Wendell Berry (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 glitch of The New Yorker:.

THE LOVED ONES by Wendell Berry.

The loved ones we call the dead depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if called back by our love, they come near us again. They enter our dreams. We feel they have been near us when we have not thought of them. They are simply here, simply waiting while we are distracted among our obligations. At last it comes to us: They live now in the permanent world. We are the absent ones.

Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s extraordinary love letter to his wife written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on creativity and love and his timeless antidote to despair.

Local tweaks gave early markets personality, yet the patchwork look left fleets reading like separate pilot programs instead of one operator. Strategy uncovered who really held the keys. Partner and Creative Director Justin Colt says New York and New Orleans studio The Collected Works stopped treating Circuit like a noisy startup. Instead, his team looked to everyday utilities like plumbing, gas, and electricity â public systems people expect to work.

In a recent development, tossing out the archive wasnât necessary. Coltâs team sharpened Circuitâs original C icon, keeping its nested street grid and directional path intact. Every market name now locks beside the wordmark the exact same way, as seen on the dark Circuit Austin pill over an Airport Blvd highway interchange. Typography handles the daily workload across dozens of markets. Public Typeâs Stadt brings sharp thick-to-thin stroke contrast to headlines alongside Displaayâs Haffer, taking cues from the New York City subway style guide. Thin map arrows sit right between words. On the metallic green rear fender wrap, hairline turn glyphs thread through âSay bye to circling the block.â Nearby touchpoints stay hyper-local: a tiled Brooklyn subway poster stacks âFrom Union Pool To Your Friends Roofâ in mint type, while a blue Boston brick mural pokes fun at Green Line delays.

Look at the dark green âWe Make the Short Trips Count.â billboard and another layer of this brand identity clicks. Wide sage-green bands with rounded street-corner turns cut straight across the display type. To keep that continuous Circuit line moving like a live route that doesnât repeat twice, the studio built a generative tool for in-house designers, paired with road-sign photo masks and snapping headline loops. Restraint matters most on the fleet wraps. Neighbors see the same shuttles parked three feet away or passing at 30 miles an hour for years. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

Sources indicate that while some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

Sources indicate that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four new practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

Let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

Years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She stated, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

While this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

This practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

As managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

Industry observers note that one study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

It has been revealed that the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an crucial part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

Recent findings suggest that in their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

We encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that an organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities.
  • Humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself. Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. And while I kiss my lover on the fresh-cut grass under the Manhattan Bridge, it goes on cloning itself as we go on dying and passing between our lips the heat of our mortality.

Recent findings suggest that an organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities. Human beings are organisms encased in the hardest yet most vulnerable exoskeleton in nature: a self. A self includes but surpasses the organism to encompass its environment and its social context, the psychological terrain of memory and desire, the fingerprints left on it by the touch of other selves. An organism ends at the physical boundary of its body, but a self does not — we spend our lives negotiating where we end and the world begins.

Humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone. We are also the only animal who can radically alter both its environment and its social context, building elaborate homes on faraway landmasses, reconstituting our families and friend groups, changing the labors by which we put food on our table. Our selves are not like our cells, replacing themselves with clones in the course of living, but like Russian nesting dolls, each prior self outgrown but contained by the next. (“We are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive manufacturer or not,” Joan Didion wrote.) Our lives a relay race, running from the selves we have outgrown or wish to outgrow towards the selves we try to become to or are unconsciously becoming, the baton of personhood passed from one to the next along the arrow of time, the track of our mortality.

In a recent development, this puts us in a peculiar predicament: Each human lifetime is lived by a single organism that contains a multitude of selves, genetically continuous and psychologically discontinuous, making it impossible to define where and what the person is. What, then, makes you yourself across all those replaced cells and reconfigured selves?

Organisms like Posidonia australis, which both conceal and reveal the nature of the self, may give us the best hint at an answer — one which evolutionary biologist Rowan Hooper articulates beautifully in his book Togetherness: Symbiosis and the Hidden Story of Life’s Greatest Collaborations (public library). Considering Earth’s largest living tree, he writes:.

The Pando aspen grove in Utah comprises 47,000 trees, all genetically identical, connected by a vast root system. Language immediately becomes limiting when trying to describe Pando. Do we call the forest an organism? An entity? It has been estimated to weigh nearly 6 million kilograms, or 6,000 tonnes. If it helps, that’s about thirty-five blue whales or 1,000 elephants. It is one of the oldest organisms on Earth. Its cells are living and dying over time, but the DNA remains pretty much unchanged. That is, the entity lives on, even as its parts die.

With an eye to the Ship of Theseus — Plutarch’s timeless thought experiment about the nature of the self — he reflects:.

Pando is biology’s Ship of Theseus — is it the same tree as when it first sprouted? I think not. It’s more like a continuation of the idea of Pando… The 47,000 stems of Pando start off genetically the same, but grow phenotypically different; a forest, but also a mass of individuals.

Industry observers note that “The word for world is forest,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her subtle insistence that symbiosis — the ultimate unselfing of the organism — is what made this rocky planet a living world. Rustling through the canopy of the Pando is the whisper of an answer to the unnerving question of what makes a body a person: You are not your roots, not the stem of your circumstance, not your branching choices. You are the idea of you, the forest of your selves in constant conviviality with other selves, called again and again to unself into who you really are.

#69042. Why Sending Reels Is More Meaningful Than You Think

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1621 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Why Sending Reels Is More Meaningful Than You Think

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most.
  • It has been revealed that this has been my experience.
  • A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most. Today, one of our most ubiquitous connection rituals is reel sharing—that is, sending short social media videos to each other. At a time when much of the conversation about technology centers on how it is eroding human connection, reel sharing and the unspoken social norms that surround it suggest another possibility: a tool to maintain social bonds.

It has been revealed that this has been my experience. I met my best friend of more than 25 years, Kyra, when I was a Peace Corps volunteer. Our friendship formed before social media and with geographic distance between us (she served in Togo and I was in Cameroon). During Peace Corps service, we mainly stayed in touch through sporadic emails. After Peace Corps, we both started careers in international development, got married, and had a few kids. Our geographic separation didn’t change, but our time to email and chat on the phone did, significantly limiting our communication. I missed her.

A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference). It became our version of “I’m thinking of you” or “Here’s something to brighten your day”—an asynchronous way of staying connected, sharing our interests, and quietly checking our emotional attunement with one another. Sending reels has helped to strengthen our friendship at a cadence that works for our busy lives.

But there’s a tension with this practice, which is the guilt I sometimes feel about spending so much time on social media. Though an estimated 37–71% of Americans use social media sites, many have turned against them altogether, inviting us to throw out both the baby and the bathwater. Indeed, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) recently settled a lawsuit (for billions of dollars) that alleged that their sites were intentionally designed to addict children and teens.

According to recent reports, there might be good reasons to restrain social media use, but people will continue to use it—and so the question becomes: How can they use it wisely? Perhaps repositioning social media reel sending as a ritual of connection can help to recalibrate how and why we engage with the platform.

Social science sees interpersonal rituals as repetitive, symbolic actions that foster belonging and communicate shared meaning. Such rituals are routinized actions or behaviors that have unspoken norms understood by the participants. Performing the ritual with others symbolizes their importance in our lives and creates an opportunity for shared meaning, which collectively reinforces the bond.

Sending reels has become a modernized form of relationship maintenance, done to keep a relationship alive, relevant, and emotionally present. Relationship maintenance is a behavior we engage in to show our commitment to a relationship. There are both routine and strategic forms of relationship maintenance. We employ these tactics across all types of relationships: romantic, platonic, familial, and professional.

Routine maintenance consist of frequent, intuitive acts done to stay connected to the person through regular communication and information sharing—as opposed to grander gestures like buying flowers and other gifts, showing up at difficult moments, or bringing someone to the airport.

In a recent development, the reason we feel irritated when our reel sending doesn’t receive a reaction is because relationships are rooted in social exchange. Essentially, relationships are based on a subconscious cost-benefit analysis, where reciprocity is expected, although not explicitly stated. Behaviors that are rewarded will continue—but the absence of reward can harm the relationship.

According to recent reports, perhaps you’re a mom who recently started sending reels to your adult daughter to reinforce regular communication. You’ll likely continue to do so until you realize, “Wait, she hasn’t responded.” While the action of sending reels is something we may do without much thought, we expect acknowledgment of the gesture: a like, emoji, comment, or reciprocal sending. When we don’t receive that, we feel disappointed. But when we do get the anticipated response, we feel closer to the person.

Kyra and I use a combination of emojis and reciprocal sending to signify reception. We’re so committed to reciprocal sending, that the other day she sent me this reel to remind me what to do if a couple of days went by without her sending me anything!

Think about the last person you sent a reel to. Who was it? I’m willing to bet they were a close friend, relative, or romantic partner. That’s because reels are typically shared with someone you care about, someone you want to be in community with, and the goal is to reinforce closeness.

While research focused on sending reels as a form of digital communication is scarce, we can extrapolate the link between relationship closeness and reel-sending behavior from studies focused on digital memes (static photos) and GIFs (looping animations).

Recent findings suggest that researchers asked 395 study participants, ranging in age from 18 to 75, to recall situations where they sent a text message to a strong tie (close relationship) and a weak tie (acquaintance) and report their use of graphic icons such as memes, GIFs, and emojis. Participants reported more sharing with strong ties than weak ties.

Those who used graphic icons more frequently reported greater feelings of self-disclosure (“I can talk to X about anything”), relationship maintenance (We “try to make each other laugh”), and intimacy (“How often do you tell your friend everything that you are going through?”).

Admittedly, sending a reel to someone requires a bit of vulnerability.

In a recent development, you are taking a risk by sending something that resonates with you, but you aren’t 100% sure will resonate and be reciprocated by the other person. The likelihood of success depends on how accurately you guessed the person’s likes or dislikes.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerability factor is another reason we are more likely to send reels to close others; vulnerability typically follows closeness, not the other way around. When we are vulnerable with people we are close to, the risk is diminished because we know them better. If it fails, the potential harm is cushioned by our established relationship.

Aside from the vulnerability factor, there’s a reason when you’re scrolling social media that you don’t see a reel and immediately think to send it to Bob in accounting or your dentist. While they may be cool people, they simply aren’t top of mind for you.

Close relationships carry emotional weight, and our brain is much more likely to remember emotionally salient information. For example, Kyra has three very active sons who all play competitive sports. Her weekends are consumed with sporting events, so every time I see a post about sports moms, I think of her and send it. It’s my way of recognizing her efforts and sacrifice.

Sources indicate that reels are digital objects that can trigger us to think of others. Because we have much more information about close relationships and cognitively our experiences with them are more accessible, when we want to share a reel, we pick from this list of people.

Shared experiences are an notable component of fostering connections, serving as the foundation for establishing shared meaning. When you’re in the same physical space, this might look like watching movies together, attending events, or sharing meals.

Reels offer an asynchronous substitute for shared experiences. By viewing a reel, and maybe even sharing a brief commentary on it, and then sending it to a connection who then reacts, you are creating a digital shared experience—viewing and reacting to the same content.

It has been revealed that shared experiences help us to understand the preferences and thoughts of others, while sharing our own. Through this exchange, we can align our minds and create shared meaning. It’s a form of emotional attunement, a core component of close social connection.

Recent findings suggest that sending reels tests out that alignment. Essentially, when we send reels, we are saying, “I found this to be funny, did you?” or “This really resonated with me, how about you?”  or “I thought this information would be useful to you, is it?” The validation of alignment is in the receiver’s reaction.

When distance or busyness prevent or limit in-person interaction, sending reels allows us to share funny, thought-provoking, or motivational content with people we care about, maintaining a sense of closeness, having laughed, gasped, or become angry at the same reel. We reinforce connection through mutual understanding and shared meaning.

If you send reels and you’ve categorized it as a “guilty pleasure,” I’d encourage you to reconsider the guilt part. Guilt suggests you are doing something bad when the intention and the value behind sending the reel is likely anything but.

The all-or-nothing culture of social media today doesn’t give space for a more nuanced look at our productive use of these platforms and overlooks that some of our online engagement reflects values-based behaviors.

In a recent development, the question is not simply how much time we spend on social media, but what we are doing there. Compulsive scrolling and intentionally connecting with someone we care about may occur on the same platform, but they are not the same.

In a recent development, so, keep sending the reels, not as the only sign that you care, but as one of many in your interpersonal toolbox. I know Kyra and I don’t proposal on stopping anytime soon!

Shanna B. Tiayon, Ph.D., also known as “The Wellbeing Dr.,” is a writer, speaker, and trainer working in the area of well-being. Presently, Shanna is the owner of WellbeingWorks, LLC, a boutique well-being firm bringing together the best interdisciplinary knowledge in the areas of social psychology, human resources, research, and training design.

True Love Will Find You in the End: Kurt Vonnegut on When to Stop Trying and When to Try Again
