📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climbing the Andes one windy January afternoon, watching peak after peek emerge on the horizon like giant mounds of moss, I found myself wondering about the clear line toward the top where the green ends and the reddish-brown of the barren rock begins, wondering how the trees and shrubs know when to stop, how far to keep pushing, where the point is past which the conditions become too inhospitable for growth, for flourishing, for survival.

It has been revealed that this may be the hardest equation to balance in all of existence: when to keep trying and when to stop. Nowhere is it more confounding, because nowhere is the calculus of reason more haunted by emotion, than in our intimate relationships. There, all the variables are too charged with feeling to be weighed accurately; there, the most vulnerable part of the ego keeps factoring itself into the arithmetic. Because time is something we can measure and tenderness is not, we keep trying to ward off the singular sense of personal failure that the loss of love can bring by measuring the success of a relationship by quantity of time rather than quality of being, only to find ourselves on barren rock.

Kurt Vonnegut (November 11, 1922–April 11, 2007) was twenty-two and just home from his wartime duty in Europe, where he had been held as a prisoner of war in Dresden and barely survived the Allied bombing of the city, when he married his college classmate Jane Marie Cox — two young people not yet having become themselves, unformed and unhealed, trying to be together.

They loved each other, but as they grew up, they grew apart, grew askance. And yet, dragged by the momentum of culture, they had a son, then a daughter, then another as Vonnegut struggled to make a living as a writer.

When his sister died of cancer two days after her husband was killed in a train accident, he adopted their three young sons. In that way life has of denying us any alternative experimental condition but our lived experience, no one knows what might have become of the couple in an experimental design other than a small house pattered by six hungry children. They fought more and more, until even the most mundane conversation couldn’t but become an argument.

Vonnegut tried to take refuge in writing, but his twin peaks of bills and rejection slips came to tower over his dream. Middle-aged and penniless, he was about to give up when he received an unexpected offer to teach at the prestigious Iowa Writers’ Workshop, procured through the kindness of a single reader touched by the work of this obscure unhappy writer. It was a lifeline both professional and personal. Vonnegut packed his bags and headed to Iowa, knowing in his heart, though he was not yet ready to allow the thought, that this was the end of his life with Jane.

Two years into teaching, as his writing was finally beginning to receive recognition, he was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship and used the prize money to travel back to Dresden, only to find much of the city still in ruins. I wonder if he thought about love then, how it too is a world that can be left in ruins beyond repair if the warfare is too brutal or too long.

Suddenly catapulted into public success — after five novels and countless short stories, Vonnegut was lauded as an overnight success with Slaughterhouse-Five — he remained lodged in the pit of personal failure. He and Jane had been together for a quarter century, happy for only a fraction of it. Torn between his emotional inability to hold on to the relationship and his cerebral unwillingness to give up, he began drowning his discontent in drink.

According to recent reports, in the last year of his forties, he moved out and headed for Newly introduced York, but couldn’t bring himself to end the marriage. Taking solace in Margaret Mead’s assurance that “a couple which has had children has an irreversible and undissolvable relationship,” he wrote to Jane:.

We hurt each other back and forth so much, almost absent-mindedly, that it was common sense for us to separate, if only to break the rhythm.

He shaded in this stark contour in a letter to a friend, painting a haunting portrait of a dead relationship:.

I myself am living alone in two rooms and a garden in Upcoming York, attempting to draw useful electricity from the millions of milling strangers around me. I am no longer living with Jane for this reason, as nearly as I can tell: We are no longer capable of conducting amiable conversations. When we try to talk, to amuse each other and pass the time, our words are wooden, stilted, queer, distant, and — finally — quietly bitter. That is too bad, and many people regard me as heartless for leaving her. But the hours and days and years dragged so. I am happier now, though far from hilarious and proud. I have achieved a sort of Limbo, which is a distinct improvement over what I had before. I am beginning to write again. That had stopped for a while. I do not wish to marry again. I’m not in love with anybody else.

It has been revealed that writing remained his one oasis of sanity amid the limbo of his Middle Passage. Some part of him — that wise part that lives in each of us, whispering what we don’t want to but need to hear — knew that he had to reimagine his life if he were not to squander it. But he was not ready. So he reimagined his writing, taking the skeleton of a play he had written fifteen years earlier and enfleshing it anew. Happy Birthday, Wanda June ran for five months to mixed reviews, but the world was finally paying attention.

Having documented Martin Luther King, Jr.’s historic speech during the March on Washington and worked as a war photographer in Vietnam, Jill Krementz was unperturbed by the cantankerous writer whose process she was hired to capture for a magazine profile. She immediately felt both Vonnegut’s brilliance and his brokenness, felt the sharp edge on which his own heart was breaking, saw to the roiling core of his wounded tenderness. He immediately decided he didn’t like her. (“There is no terror like that of being known,” Emerson shuddered at the discomposing intimacy that bloomed between him and Margaret Fuller.).

Within months, they were living together.

Just before he moved in with Jill, Vonnegut wrote to his seventeen-year-old daughter Nanette:.

You certainly deserve a letter from me. A hundred letters would be more like it, I love you so.

I will be home from time to time to see you. But I will not stay for long. I still love your mother, but we can’t be together much without fighting. We have tried to do things about this, but nothing helps, and each fight hurts more than the last one.

In a recent development, I wasn’t stolen away by another woman. I don’t think people can steal other people. I simply went away because the fighting was making everybody so unhappy. I’ve done that several times before. Going to Iowa was an example. Every time I went away I simply went to aloneness. There was never any other woman beckoning me to come.

Recent findings suggest that this time, for instance, I couldn’t make myself come home after the play opened, and I was alone. I hardly knew Jill at all, and I didn’t like her much, and whatever happened between us happened long after I’d decided home was too uncomfortable for me.

Recent findings suggest that eighteen years his junior but in many ways his spiritual elder, Jill enveloped him in a kindness so entirely fresh he didn’t know what to do with it, a love he hadn’t thought possible. He tried to fight with her, out of reflex, but she simply loved him, and so he slowly unbraced the oppositional stance that had become his default, slowly stopped self-medicating. He grew healthy, grew happy, grew himself.

In a recent development, still, it took him six years to meet the emotional truth of his failed marriage with the hard fact of divorce. When he finally decided to do it, he wrote to Nan:.

It has been revealed that as for the divorce: I will always love your mother, as must have been evident on Sunday. But we could never live together again. Our conversations go so badly. Also: I want to be fair to Jill, who saved me from knocking myself off or turning into an alcoholic. I will not marry Jill, but I will stop asking that she live with a married man. And Jane, who is fond of marriage, should have the chance to marry again. I am not pursuing happiness through divorce. I am permanently damaged by the break-up of marriage. Those wounds will never heal. I am simply trying to make the best of an unpleasant situation. Let me say again, too, that Jill did not break the marriage. It was broken long before that — about the time I went to Iowa. There was no other woman beckoning me to Iowa. Later on, there was no woman beckoning me to Fresh York City. I arrived both places in total solitude, and feeling simply awful.

Sources indicate that there will be no acrimonious argle-bargle about divorce this time. We will not make the mistake of hiring two strangers to fight each other on our behalf. Jane and I will arrive at some sort of division of property, and some scheme for my sending her money regularly. She already owns the Cape house and some stocks and a large savings account in cash. I will add to that treasure, so she won’t have much to worry about as long as I’m popular and productive. Then Don Farber will draw up a simple agreement, and that will be that. The legal steps will be brief formalities, without any arguments to be made before a judge.

It took him another two years to formalize his relationship with Jill. By the time they decided to marry, he was fifty-seven and one of the most beloved authors in America. His daughter was the first person he told:.

Recent findings suggest that I want you to be the first person in our family to find this out: That Jill and I have decided to marry each other in November, probably a couple of days after Thanksgiving. Jill will then be three months shy of being forty, and we will have lived together about nine years. The first years of the relationship were tempestuous. Much of the tempest was my fault, surely. I was in a frenzied state of mourning and dismay over the failure of my once good marriage to Jane. Jill had nothing to do with that failure, but she was handy to blame. Be that as it may, Jill and I behave most affectionately and reasonably toward each other now, and unselfishly. We are in love. Our heads are clear. We are working and playing most cheerfully.

I do not endorse serial marriage for anyone. I myself have always wished to be as monogamous as a swan. I was monogamous with your mother until the very end, and will be so with Jill.

After a rough sketch of the wedding (“It will be very private. We don’t want our pictures in the paper.”), he added:.

Sources indicate that I sympathize fully with the mixed loyalties you and all the rest of my children would feel on such an occasion. So I of course invite you all, and hope you all will come. If the ceremony and party are going to cause you pain, you should not subject yourself to that pain. Your coming or staying away will not be a vote for or against anything.

Mostly, dear Nanny, I want you to know how happy I am just now, and that I have every reason to look forward to some very good years ahead.

Kurt and Jill remained together until his death, thirty-six years after they met. It was there, in the safety and sweetness of their love, that he discovered the simple secret of happiness.

#69040. Latest Update: How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

Latest Update: How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care.
  • Recent findings suggest that positive psychologists often act like that.
  • While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

Recent findings suggest that positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

According to recent reports, consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

It has been revealed that how best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks issues such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

In a recent development, however, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

Why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks problems have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

Industry observers note that that’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

It has been revealed that as a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

It has been revealed that thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy problems are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

Industry observers note that one of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

It has been revealed that indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

Misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

Sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

In a recent development, positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

Industry observers note that in our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:.

Their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:.

According to recent reports, initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

We’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

You can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

Let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

That potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind users of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

Roger G. Tweed, Ph.D., is an instructor in psychology at Douglas College.

#69039. Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh

Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.
  • According to recent reports, vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers.
  • As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing upcoming and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.

According to recent reports, vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.

As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing upcoming and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”.

Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.

Vanessa Bell’s portrait Roger Fry (1912).

© National Portrait Gallery, London.

In a recent development, as so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.

Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.

Sources indicate that the Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.

It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

The impact of Post-Impressionism: Duncan Grant's The Mantelpiece (1914) and Vanessa Bell's Still Life on Corner of a Mantelpiece (1914).

Industry observers note that grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s Newly introduced Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.

The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.

Van Gogh’s Bouquet of Flowers (summer 1886).

private collection (formerly Galerie Schmit, Paris).

Post-Impressionism and Provence.

But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.

This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a latest life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”.

Catalogue of the second Post-Impressionist catalogue (1912), co-designed by Bell, Grant and Fry.

Bibliothèque de l'Institut National d'Histoire de l'Art, Jacques Doucet collections.

In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.

Duncan Grant’s South of France (1920).

© Tate. Photo © Tate (Joe Humphrys).

How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.

The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).

Recent findings suggest that the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.

Sources indicate that decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

Recent findings suggest that martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

In a recent development, his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.
